claim: HemK NTD consists of 72 amino acids arranged into five α-helices (H1 to H5) in a globular domain.
source: Native folded HemK NTD (72 amino acids (aa)) consists of five α-helices (H1 to H5) arranged into a globular domain, identical to the NTD conformation in the full HemK protein (Yang et al., 2004; Figure 1a).
evidence: Directly stated in the text with citation to Yang et al., 2004 and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: HemK NTD folds in solution at a rate of 5 ms⁻¹.
source: In solution this domain folds at a rate of 5 ms⁻¹ while the translation rate for HemK NTD is 3.6 amino acids s⁻¹ (Holtkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: The translation rate for HemK NTD is 3.6 amino acids s⁻¹.
source: In solution this domain folds at a rate of 5 ms⁻¹ while the translation rate for HemK NTD is 3.6 amino acids s⁻¹ (Holtkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: The ribosomal peptide exit tunnel is approximately 100 Å long.
source: The growing peptide moves from the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) of the ribosome into the peptide exit tunnel, which is ~100 Å long and ~20 Å wide at the vestibule where the nascent peptide emerges into the cytoplasm.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The ribosomal peptide exit tunnel is approximately 20 Å wide at the vestibule.
source: The growing peptide moves from the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) of the ribosome into the peptide exit tunnel, which is ~100 Å long and ~20 Å wide at the vestibule where the nascent peptide emerges into the cytoplasm.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The narrowest part of the exit tunnel (constriction site) is approximately 30 Å away from the PTC.
source: The narrowest part of the tunnel – the constriction site – is ~30 Å away from the PTC and about 10 Å wide (Nissen et al., 2000).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Nissen et al., 2000.

claim: The constriction site of the exit tunnel is about 10 Å wide.
source: The narrowest part of the tunnel – the constriction site – is ~30 Å away from the PTC and about 10 Å wide (Nissen et al., 2000).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Nissen et al., 2000.

claim: The dimensions of the exit tunnel generally prevent formation of complex tertiary interactions.
source: The dimensions of the exit tunnel generally prevent formation of complex tertiary interactions.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: Some secondary and tertiary structures can form inside specific folding zones of the exit tunnel.
source: However, studies using Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) (Woolhead et al., 2004; Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018; Khushoo et al., 2011), cysteine accessibility assays (Lu and Deutsch, 2005; Kosolapov and Deutsch, 2009; Tu et al., 2014), and cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Bhushan et al., 2010; Javed et al., 2017; Nilsson et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Nilsson et al., 2017) of ribosome–nascent-chain complexes (RNCs) have shown that some secondary and tertiary structures can form inside specific folding zones of the exit tunnel.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to FRET, cysteine accessibility, and cryo-EM studies.

claim: The upper part of the exit tunnel from the PTC to the constriction can accommodate α-helices.
source: The upper part of the tunnel from the PTC to the constriction can accommodate α-helices, whereas the lower part of the tunnel, past the constriction, allows secondary and tertiary hairpin structures to form.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The lower part of the exit tunnel, past the constriction, allows secondary and tertiary hairpin structures to form.
source: The upper part of the tunnel from the PTC to the constriction can accommodate α-helices, whereas the lower part of the tunnel, past the constriction, allows secondary and tertiary hairpin structures to form.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The ribosome can alter the folding pathway of a protein from concerted to sequential.
source: It can alter the folding pathway of a protein from concerted to sequential, driven by the vectorial appearance of structural elements in the exit tunnel (Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018)
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Holtkamp et al., 2015 and Mercier and Rodnina, 2018.

claim: The ribosome can induce helical and random-coil behavior of nascent peptide.
source: induce helical and random-coil behavior of nascent peptide, alter the folding rates, and facilitate the correct folding of nascent chains (Kaiser et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Alexander et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Kaiser et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Alexander et al., 2019.

claim: The nascent chain can form a near-native compact structure while still bound to the ribosome upon emerging from the tunnel.
source: Upon emerging from the tunnel, the nascent chain can form a near-native compact structure while still bound to the ribosome (Khushoo et al., 2011; Nilsson et al., 2017; Waudby et al., 2018; Cabrita et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Samelson et al., 2018; Farías-Rico et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated with multiple citations.

claim: The ribosome can significantly destabilize folded globular proteins in its vicinity.
source: The ribosome can significantly destabilize folded globular proteins in its vicinity (Kaiser et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Alexander et al., 2019)
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Kaiser et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Alexander et al., 2019.

claim: Protein stability can be restored by extending the linker and allowing the protein to move further away from the ribosome surface.
source: the stability can be restored by extending the linker and allowing the protein to move further away from the ribosome surface (Cabrita et al., 2016; Samelson et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Cabrita et al., 2016 and Samelson et al., 2016.

claim: A 17 amino acids-long translational arrest peptide SecM is sufficient to stall translation in the absence of any additional mechanical force.
source: In the absence of any additional mechanical force, a 17 amino acids (aa)-long translational arrest peptide, SecM, is sufficient to stall translation (Ito and Chiba, 2013).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Ito and Chiba, 2013.

claim: A high-tension mechanical pulling force (7–16 pN) originating from nascent protein folding can alleviate SecM stalling and restart translation.
source: A high-tension mechanical pulling force (7–16 pN) originating from nascent protein folding (Goldman et al., 2015; Kemp et al., 2020), can alleviate the SecM stalling and restart translation (Nilsson et al., 2015; Ismail et al., 2012; Goldman et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Goldman et al., 2015; Kemp et al., 2020; Nilsson et al., 2015; Ismail et al., 2012.

claim: FPA-derived folding trajectories are consistent with FRET, PET, NMR, and cryo-EM analyses of cotranslational protein folding.
source: FPA-derived folding trajectories are consistent with FRET, PET, NMR, and cryo-EM analyses of cotranslational protein folding (Holtkamp et al., 2015; Nilsson et al., 2015; Cabrita et al., 2016; Kemp et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: FPA can identify folding events at single-codon resolution.
source: FPA can identify folding events at single-codon resolution, but this potential has not been utilized so far in identifying early folding intermediates inside the peptide exit tunnel.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: PET requires short-range interactions (van der Waals contacts, <1 nm) between quencher and dye.
source: PET requires short-range interactions (van der Waals contacts,<1 nm) between quencher and dye, which allows to specifically monitor local structural fluctuations of protein chains.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: HemK NTD folds independently of the C-terminal domain in solution.
source: We have chosen the NTD as a model protein because in solution it folds independently of the C-terminal domain and its folding on the ribosome differs dramatically from the two-state concerted folding of the free protein in solution (Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018; Kemp et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018; Kemp et al., 2019.

claim: HemK NTD folding on the ribosome differs dramatically from the two-state concerted folding of the free protein in solution.
source: We have chosen the NTD as a model protein because in solution it folds independently of the C-terminal domain and its folding on the ribosome differs dramatically from the two-state concerted folding of the free protein in solution (Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018; Kemp et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018; Kemp et al., 2019.

claim: Cotranslational folding of HemK NTD proceeds sequentially through several compact intermediates.
source: The cotranslational folding pathway is not known in detail, but FRET and PET studies suggest that cotranslational folding of HemK NTD proceeds sequentially through several compact intermediates (Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018)
evidence: Stated as suggested by FRET and PET studies with citations to Holtkamp et al., 2015 and Mercier and Rodnina, 2018.

claim: The observed folding dynamics is rapid compared to the pace of translation.
source: Furthermore, previous time-resolved experiments showed that the observed folding dynamics is rapid compared to the pace of translation, and that the nascent chains arrested at different stages of translation (stalled RNCs) faithfully reflect the dynamics that occurs during synthesis (Holtkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: Nascent chains arrested at different stages of translation (stalled RNCs) faithfully reflect the dynamics that occurs during synthesis.
source: Furthermore, previous time-resolved experiments showed that the observed folding dynamics is rapid compared to the pace of translation, and that the nascent chains arrested at different stages of translation (stalled RNCs) faithfully reflect the dynamics that occurs during synthesis (Holtkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: High-resolution FPA reveals several distinct force-generating folding events starting early inside the exit tunnel until the entire NTD emerges from the ribosome.
source: The detailed force profile of the HemK NTD reveals several distinct force-generating folding events starting early inside the exit tunnel until the entire NTD emerges from the ribosome (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: Early high-tension regions are observed at nascent-chain lengths of aa 22–24 (I), 33–39 (II) and 42–52 (III) with a transient force relief at aa 48.
source: The early high-tension regions are observed at nascent-chain lengths of aa 22–24 (I), 33–39 (II) and 42–52 (III) with a transient force relief at aa 48.
evidence: Directly stated in the text describing FPA results.

claim: At nascent-chain lengths of 22-24 aa, 33-39 aa, and 42-52 aa, the nascent peptide is likely to reside in the exit tunnel as it is protected from protease digestion.
source: At these chain lengths, the nascent peptide is likely to reside in the exit tunnel, as it is protected from protease digestion (Holtkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: Introducing prolines into the 22–32 region leads to a flattening of the FPA profile.
source: Introducing prolines into the 22–32 region leads to a flattening of the FPA profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g)
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: If the polypeptide is truncated within the loop between H1 and H2, tension is abolished.
source: Furthermore, if the polypeptide is truncated within the loop between H1 and H2, tension is abolished (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The entire first loop sequence together with H1 are necessary to create the high-tension event at region I.
source: suggesting that the entire first loop sequence together with H1 are necessary to create the high-tension event.
evidence: Stated as a suggestion based on experimental data.

claim: Proline substitutions in the 34–38 region decrease tension considerably.
source: Proline substitutions in the 34–38 region decrease tension considerably (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g)
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Region III at aa 42–52 broadly coincides with the compacted intermediate identified by FRET and FPA studies.
source: Region III at aa 42–52 (Figure 1c,d) broadly coincides with the compacted intermediate identified by FRET and FPA studies (Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018; Kemp et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to Holtkamp et al., 2015; Mercier and Rodnina, 2018; Kemp et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 1c,d.

claim: Proline mutations abolish formation of the high-tension peak at region III.
source: Proline mutations abolish formation of the high-tension peak (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: The H1-H3 intermediate structure is expected to reside approximately 50–60 Å away from the PTC in the region within the exit tunnel.
source: The H1-H3 intermediate structure is expected to reside approximately 50–60 Å away from the PTC in the region within the exit tunnel that is known to accommodate a folded small zinc-finger domain protein (ADR1) (Nilsson et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Nilsson et al., 2015.

claim: The HemK H1-H3 intermediate and ADR1 domain are of similar size.
source: The two domains are of similar size (Figure 1e)
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1e.

claim: The folding intermediate of H1-H3 can be accommodated in the region of the tunnel where ADR1 resides.
source: even if the HemK H1-H3 occupies a slightly larger volume than ADR1, it is very likely that the folding intermediate of H1-H3 can be accommodated in this region of the tunnel.
evidence: Stated as very likely based on structural comparison.

claim: When the nascent chain reaches the total length of 84 aa, position 34 is no longer protected by the ribosome.
source: Protease protection experiments suggest that when the nascent chain reaches the total length of 84 aa, position 34 (fluorescently labeled in those experiments) is no longer protected by the ribosome (Holtkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as suggested by protease protection experiments with citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: The next high-tension intermediate at aa 72–78 (region V) forms when H5 and part of the following interdomain linker move past the constriction and H4 is further displaced toward the vestibule.
source: The next high-tension intermediate at aa 72–78 (region V) forms when H5 and part of the following interdomain linker move past the constriction and H4 is further displaced toward the vestibule.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The final high-tension compaction (step VII) occurs when the length of the HemK NTD exceeds 86 aa, placing the entire NTD outside of the confines of the exit tunnel.
source: The final high-tension compaction (step VII) occurs when the length of the HemK NTD exceeds 86 aa, placing the entire NTD, H1 through H5, outside of the confines of the exit tunnel (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1c,d.

claim: When NTD length is >95 aa (112 aa total peptide length), only basal tension levels are observed.
source: When NTD length is >95 aa (112 aa total peptide length), we observe only basal tension levels, indicating that the final cotranslational folding to a near-native conformation of the NTD occurred at step VII
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The 4xA variant has four conserved Leu residues of the hydrophobic core (Leu 27 and 28 in H2, and 55 and 58 in H4) mutated to Ala.
source: In addition to the wt HemK NTD, we examined cotranslational folding of the destabilized HemK NTD variant (4xA), where four conserved Leu residues of the hydrophobic core (Leu 27 and 28 in H2, and 55 and 58 in H4) were mutated to Ala (Figure 1a; Holtkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1a and citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: The force profile inside the exit tunnel is identical for the wt and the 4xA variant (folding steps I-III).
source: The force profile inside the exit tunnel is identical for the wt and the 4xA variant (folding steps I-III), but as the peptide begins to emerge at the vestibule, the force profiles start to deviate (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,e).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,e.

claim: As the peptide begins to emerge at the vestibule, the force profiles of wt and 4xA start to deviate.
source: The force profile inside the exit tunnel is identical for the wt and the 4xA variant (folding steps I-III), but as the peptide begins to emerge at the vestibule, the force profiles start to deviate (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,e).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,e.

claim: For the 4xA variant, there is a drop in tension at a total length of 73 aa (56 aa of HemK NTD).
source: For the 4xA variant, we observe a drop in tension at a total length of 73 aa (56 aa of HemK NTD), and the appearance of a high-force intermediate at a chain length where the tension in the wt HemK NTD gradually decreases (aa 62–64) (region IV).
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The 4xA variant shows appearance of a high-force intermediate at aa 62–64 where the tension in the wt HemK NTD gradually decreases.
source: For the 4xA variant, we observe a drop in tension at a total length of 73 aa (56 aa of HemK NTD), and the appearance of a high-force intermediate at a chain length where the tension in the wt HemK NTD gradually decreases (aa 62–64) (region IV).
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The two following cotranslational folding steps V and VII are similar in duration and amplitude for 4xA and wt.
source: The two following cotranslational folding steps V and VII are similar in duration and amplitude for 4xA and wt, suggesting that these rearrangements are independent of the hydrophobic core packing.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: In regions VI and VIII, the 4xA variant generates consistently higher tension than the wt NTD.
source: In contrast, in regions VI and VIII, the 4xA variant generates consistently higher tension than the wt NTD.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The native Trp6 residue in HemK can quench an N-terminal ATTO655 fluorophore upon coming into van der Waals distance.
source: We utilized the native Trp6 residue (W6) in HemK that could quench an N-terminal ATTO655 fluorophore upon coming into van der Waals distance (Doose et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Doose et al., 2009.

claim: The isolated W6F HemK NTD variant is 90% folded at 37°C compared to the wt.
source: The isolated W6F HemK NTD variant is 90% folded at 37°C compared to the wt and has the same translation rate and profile (Holtkamp et al., 2015)
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Holtkamp et al., 2015.

claim: FCS measurements of the isolated NTD showed a stable and highly reproducible diffusion time of the peptide (τd1 ≈ 6 × 10−5 s).
source: FCS measurements of the isolated NTD showed a stable and highly reproducible diffusion time of the peptide (τd1 ≈ 6 × 10−5 s) (Supplementary file 1 - table 1).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 1 - table 1.

claim: No PET signal was observed for isolated NTD, as the autocorrelation functions (ACF) with W6 and W6F proteins are identical for wt and 4xA constructs.
source: However, no PET signal was observed, as the autocorrelation functions (ACF) with W6 and W6F proteins are identical for wt and 4xA constructs (Figure 2a).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: There are no dynamic fluctuations at the N-terminus of the HemK NTD in solution.
source: This result indicates that there are no dynamic fluctuations at the N-terminus of the HemK NTD in solution.
evidence: Stated as an indication from the experimental results.

claim: Fast dynamics due to PET with a quenching relaxation time of ~5×10−7 s was observed for a short HemK peptide of 14 aa in the presence of glycerol.
source: After testing different conditions, we were able to observe fast dynamics due to PET with a quenching relaxation time of ~5×10−7 s in the presence of glycerol (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 1 - table 1).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2b and Supplementary file 1 - table 1.

claim: In solution, HemK NTD and its destabilized 4xA variant fold into a domain where W6 is not accessible for interaction with the N-terminal dye.
source: Thus, in solution, HemK NTD, as well as its destabilized 4xA variant, folds into a domain where W6 is not accessible for interaction with the N-terminal dye.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: PET-FCS experiments with ribosome complexes are complicated by Trp residues in ribosomal proteins and guanines of the rRNA that also quench the N-terminal fluorophore.
source: One complication of the PET-FCS experiments with ribosome complexes is that the Trp residues in ribosomal proteins and guanines of the rRNA also quench the N-terminal fluorophore (Doose et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Doose et al., 2009.

claim: For all RNCs tested, PET-FCS experiments yield multiphasic ACFs spanning the timescale from ms to ns.
source: For all RNCs tested, PET-FCS experiments yield multiphasic ACFs spanning the timescale from ms to ns.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: Initial exponential fitting reveals at least three fast dynamic components in the μs time range.
source: Initial exponential fitting reveals at least three fast dynamic components in the μs time range.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: One of the components most likely reflects the triplet state pumping and relaxation of the ATTO655 dye in the complex with the ribosome.
source: One of the components most likely reflects the triplet state pumping and relaxation of the ATTO655 dye in the complex with the ribosome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as most likely with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relaxation time of the triplet state of ATTO655 attached to the peptide on the ribosome is about 40 µs.
source: The relaxation time of the triplet state of ATTO655 attached to the peptide on the ribosome, about 40 µs, is somewhat larger than that measured with a model peptide, which is in the range of 2 µs (Luitz et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Luitz et al., 2017.

claim: Two relaxation times (τ = 1/k), one in the tens of µs and the other in the µs time range, were observed in all tested complexes, regardless of the presence of the W6 residue.
source: The two relaxation times (τ = 1/k) as estimated by fitting, one in the tens of µs and the other in the µs time range, were observed in all tested complexes, regardless of the presence of the W6 residue that causes intra-chain PET (Supplementary file 1 - table 2).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 1 - table 2.

claim: The τ1 and τ2 values and the respective amplitudes are different for the respective W6 and W6F constructs.
source: However, the τ1 and τ2 values and the respective amplitudes are different for the respective W6 and W6F constructs, indicating that part of the effect is due to intra-chain PET.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The shorter relaxation time τ1 most likely reflects the quenching interactions of the fluorophore with the internal Trp or the quenchers at the ribosome surface.
source: Taking into account the known timescales of peptide dynamics in solution (Neuweiler et al., 2010; Luitz et al., 2017; Lum et al., 2012), the shorter relaxation time τ1 most likely reflects the quenching interactions of the fluorophore with the internal Trp or the quenchers at the ribosome surface.
evidence: Stated as most likely based on known timescales with citations.

claim: The slower relaxation time τ2 is usually attributed to the dynamics of conformational intermediates.
source: The slower relaxation time τ2 is usually attributed to the dynamics of conformational intermediates.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: Both τ1 and τ2 values are affected by loop mutations that extend a loop between H3 and H4 by five additional Gly residues.
source: Both τ1 and τ2 values are affected by the loop mutations (Supplementary file 1 - table 2).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 1 - table 2.

claim: The minimal model that can fit the ACF dataset must include five-equilibria (model 5e-H and model 5e-O).
source: We find that the minimal model that can fit our ACF dataset must include five-equilibria (model 5e-H and model 5e-O) and models with fewer equilibria are insufficient (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Global fit of the Trp titration data to the five-equilibria models yielded ATTO655–Trp dequenching rate of about 2 μs⁻¹.
source: Global fit of the Trp titration data to the five-equilibria models (Materials and methods) yielded ATTO655–Trp dequenching rate of about 2 μs⁻¹ (Supplementary file 1 - tables 3 and 4).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 1 - tables 3 and 4.

claim: The two structural states of the nascent chain, C and D, are very different with respect to their dynamics.
source: Comparison of the rate constants for different complexes reveals, first, that the two structural states of the nascent chain, C and D, are very different with respect to their dynamics (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1 - table 5).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1 - table 5.

claim: The rate constants of ATTO655 quenching by the ribosome is 20–50-fold slower in C compared to D in different RNCs.
source: The rate constants of ATTO655 quenching by the ribosome is 20–50-fold slower in C compared to D in different RNCs.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: Quenching by intramolecular Trp6 is 80–200-fold slower in C than in D.
source: Likewise, quenching by intramolecular Trp6 is 80–200-fold slower in C than in D.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: For a given conformational state C or D, the rates of interaction with Trp or the ribosome are almost insensitive to the extent of folding or the position of the N-terminus on the ribosome.
source: The second observation is that for a given conformational state C or D, the rates of interaction with Trp or the ribosome are almost insensitive to the extent of folding or the position of the N-terminus on the ribosome, as the kon value for Trp quenching is about 0.04 µs−1 for state C and 3–8 µs−1 for state D of all constructs.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The kon for ribosome quenching is not strongly dependent on the position of the nascent chain with respect to the ribosome, with kon = 0.24 µs−1 for state C and ranging from 5 μs⁻¹ to 11 μs⁻¹ for state D.
source: More surprisingly, the kon for ribosome quenching is not strongly dependent on the position of the nascent chain with respect to the ribosome, with kon = 0.24 µs−1 for state C and ranging from 5 μs⁻¹ to 11 μs⁻¹ for state D.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The dequenching rate of the ATTO655–ribosome complex is 0.3 μs⁻¹ and identical for 5e-H and 5e-O kinetic models.
source: The dequenching rate of the ATTO655–ribosome complex is 0.3 μs⁻¹ and identical for 5e-H and 5e-O kinetic models (Supplementary file 1 - tables 5 and 6).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 1 - tables 5 and 6.

claim: The compact state C is favored in all complexes.
source: The compact state C is favored in all complexes, but the rate constants of the C↔D transitions differ dramatically, decreasing with increasing protein length and its emergence outside the ribosome (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1 - table 5).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1 - table 5.

claim: The rate constants of the C↔D transitions differ dramatically, decreasing with increasing protein length and its emergence outside the ribosome.
source: The compact state C is favored in all complexes, but the rate constants of the C↔D transitions differ dramatically, decreasing with increasing protein length and its emergence outside the ribosome (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1 - table 5).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1 - table 5.

claim: The 4xA mutations in the hydrophobic core do not alter the equilibrium between the C and D states for HemK70 and HemK112.
source: The 4xA mutations in the hydrophobic core do not alter the equilibrium between the C and D states (HemK70 and HemK112), but when the domain emerges from the ribosome the mutations cause several orders of magnitude increase of the rate constants between these states (HemK112) (Figure 4).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4.

claim: When the domain emerges from the ribosome, the 4xA mutations cause several orders of magnitude increase of the rate constants between C and D states for HemK112.
source: The 4xA mutations in the hydrophobic core do not alter the equilibrium between the C and D states (HemK70 and HemK112), but when the domain emerges from the ribosome the mutations cause several orders of magnitude increase of the rate constants between these states (HemK112) (Figure 4).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Introducing a loop of 6 aa dramatically increases the rates of transitions between C and D states in both HemK102 and HemK112.
source: Furthermore, introducing a loop of 6 aa dramatically increases the rates of transitions in both HemK102 and HemK112 (Figure 4).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Loop extensions increase the helix dynamics of the nascent chain, but do not alter the interaction with Trp or the ribosome surface.
source: Thus, as predicted (Dagan et al., 2013), the loop extensions increase the helix dynamics of the nascent chain, but do not alter the interaction with Trp or the ribosome surface.
evidence: Stated as predicted with citation to Dagan et al., 2013.

claim: High-resolution FPA data show that nascent chains undergo sequential force-generating rearrangements that start inside the exit tunnel.
source: In this work, we combined FPA and PET-FCS to reconstruct the trajectory of cotranslational folding and to evaluate the stability of the folding intermediates. The high-resolution FPA data show that nascent chains undergo sequential force-generating rearrangements that start inside the exit tunnel.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: The earliest detected force-generating folding intermediate entails as little as a single helix (H1) of the HemK NTD.
source: The earliest detected force-generating folding intermediate entails as little as a single helix (H1) of the HemK NTD.
evidence: Directly stated in the text.

claim: Upon continued synthesis, emerging helices begin to interact with one another forming tertiary intermediates inside the peptide exit tunnel.
source: Upon continued synthesis, emerging helices begin to interact with one another forming tertiary intermediates inside the peptide exit tunnel (Figure 1d).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1d.

claim: The formation of individual α-helices and tertiary interactions between α-helical elements within the exit tunnel are well documented.
source: The formation of individual α-helices and tertiary interactions between α-helical elements within the exit tunnel are well documented (Lu and Deutsch, 2005; Bhushan et al., 2010; Nilsson et al., 2015; Farías-Rico et al., 2018; Nissley and O'Brien, 2018).

claim: Folding of HemK NTD is sequential.
